guides.title: Asbestos-free assurance for an imported vehicle
guides.summary: Australia bans importing anything containing asbestos, at any level, and the ABF actively targets imported cars and parts. As the owner you must be sure the car contains no asbestos before it ships. If the ABF flags your car you must give evidence; if that is not enough it will direct sampling and testing at the border at your cost, and asbestos parts are seized.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (Department of Home Affairs), with the Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency
guides.timeframe: No fixed timeframe. Sort it out in Japan before shipping; a border hold for sampling and testing adds days to weeks of storage and delay.
guides.cost_summary: No government fee. You pay for any parts replacement, technical evidence, sampling by an independent competent person, NATA-accredited testing, and storage while held.
before_you_start: The ban applies to every vehicle regardless of type, age, value or country of origin, and to temporary imports. Japan banning asbestos does not mean a Japanese car is free of it; aftermarket parts are a common source.

List the high-risk parts the ABF names: brake pads and shoes, clutch linings, gaskets (cylinder head, extractors, exhaust), seals (fuel tank, mastic, windows), bonnet liners, heater and air conditioner housings, fibrous washers, sound deadening, firewalls, heat shields, wiring wrap, body seam sealers, bituminous coatings and insulation.

Decide your assurance route before shipping: technical evidence from the manufacturer that OEM parts are asbestos-free, records of replacing at-risk parts with documented asbestos-free parts, or an accredited test report that clearly links to this specific car and the parts tested.
A seller's, supplier's or mechanic's informal statement is not enough evidence. 'Asbestos-free' labels under overseas standards may still allow low levels that are illegal here.
Keep every record (work orders, parts invoices, test reports) and make sure they name the VIN or chassis number. The ABF can ask for them at any time.

steps.title: Assess the car's risk
steps.detail: Consider age, make, model, maintenance history and any aftermarket parts. Older cars and cars with replaced brakes, clutches or gaskets are higher risk. Ask your exporter or the selling dealer for service history.

steps.title: Remove or test suspect parts in Japan
steps.detail: The ABF prefers testing or removing suspect parts before shipment, and notes that replacing them may be cheaper than sampling and testing. Keep work records and evidence of the make, model and composition of replacement parts. Overseas sampling and testing must meet Australian laboratory reporting requirements.

steps.title: Make an honest declaration
steps.detail: Only make a 'no asbestos' declaration if you are certain, covering OEM and aftermarket parts and naturally contaminated materials. Your customs broker will ask about asbestos when lodging the import declaration.

steps.title: Respond if the ABF flags the car
steps.detail: If the ABF considers the car at risk, you (or your broker) must give sufficient assurance with documents. If the evidence is not enough, the ABF directs sampling and testing at the border and supervises it while the car is under customs control.
steps.timeframe: Depends on how fast you supply evidence

steps.title: Arrange sampling and NATA-accredited testing if directed
steps.detail: You must engage a qualified, independent competent person to identify and sample suspect parts; the ABF does not take samples or remove asbestos. Analysis in Australia must be by a NATA-accredited laboratory. Storage costs while waiting are yours whether or not asbestos is found.
steps.cost: You pay sampling, testing and storage

steps.title: Deal with any positive result
steps.detail: Goods found to contain asbestos are seized and forfeited for disposal. Asbestos parts must be removed under ABF control before the car can be released, and you may face penalties.

contacts.name: Australian Border Force
contacts.note: Number as listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet. Valuation questions: valuation@abf.gov.au.

contacts.name: Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency
contacts.note: As listed in the ABF vehicle asbestos factsheet (November 2022).

watch_out: Zero tolerance: any level of asbestos is prohibited, including chrysotile (white) asbestos, and 'undisturbed' asbestos is not treated as safe.

Penalties under the Customs Act: section 233 up to 1,000 penalty units or three times the value of the goods, whichever is greater; section 233BAA up to 1,000 penalty units and/or 5 years' imprisonment; companies up to 5,000 penalty units or 15 times the value. The ABF can also issue infringement notices.
All delay, storage, sampling and testing costs fall on you, even if the test comes back clear.
Enthusiast car shows do not count as 'display', so you cannot get a permit to import an asbestos-containing car you plan to drive or show.
Aftermarket brake pads, clutch kits and gaskets bought cheaply overseas are a common cause of detections.
The ABF lists recent detections in imported cars, including a 1971 Mazda RX-2, so older Japanese cars are not exempt.

guides.title: Biosecurity cleaning and inspection for an imported used vehicle
guides.summary: Every used car arriving in Australia gets a full biosecurity inspection inside and out before release. It must arrive free of soil, mud, plant material, insects and animal waste, or it will be cleaned, fumigated, exported or destroyed at your cost. Japan is on the brown marmorated stink bug (BMSB) lists for vessel surveillance and random onshore inspection from 1 September to 30 April.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF)
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Inspection is booked after arrival through the local DAFF office at the port; usually days, longer if the car fails and needs cleaning or treatment.
guides.cost_summary: A$71 biosecurity charge on the full import declaration (sea), plus inspection time at A$42 per 15 minutes in-office or A$70 per 15 minutes out-of-office in ordinary hours (2026-27), plus any cleaning or treatment.
before_you_start: You are responsible for the car's cleanliness, inside and out, before it arrives. Risk material includes live insects, soil, mud, animal faeces, leaves, twigs, bark and seeds.
Check the wheels, wheel guards, mud guards, engine bay, underside and chassis rails, boot and spare tyre well, storage compartments, seats and seat folds, vents, and window and door seals.

Consider using a recognised offshore cleaning and pre-inspection provider (ROCIP) in Japan. Fully approved facilities get a 5% onshore verification rate instead of a full inspection. In September 2025 DAFF listed 17 approved facilities in Japan (JEVIC, Autoterminal Japan, Automotive Technologies, Bordercheck Japan, FF Forwarding) in Yokohama, Nagoya, Osaka, Kobe, Kisarazu, Kuwana, Yatomi and Kitakyushu.
Remove personal effects, loose items, used tyres or parts packed with dirt; leave the keys with the car so officers can open all compartments.
Check BICON (the Biosecurity Import Conditions system) for your goods if you are also shipping parts, tyres or other items in the container.

steps.title: Clean the car thoroughly before export
steps.detail: Steam clean the underside, wheel arches and engine bay and vacuum the interior, or book a ROCIP-approved facility in Japan to clean and pre-inspect it and issue certification. The department's 8 steps guide says to steam clean the vehicle inside and out before shipping.

steps.title: Check BMSB season rules for your shipping date
steps.detail: BMSB measures apply to targeted goods shipped from target risk countries between 1 September and 30 April (shipped-on-board date). Vehicles (tariff chapter 87) are target high risk goods needing mandatory treatment when shipped from target risk countries. Japan is listed as a target risk country for heightened vessel surveillance only, and as an emerging risk country, so goods shipped from Japan in that period may be selected for random onshore inspection. Ro-Ro ships that call at target risk countries also face a mandatory seasonal pest inspection on arrival.

steps.title: Make sure biosecurity is covered in the import declaration
steps.detail: Your customs broker's full import declaration is referred for biosecurity assessment and attracts the sea cargo biosecurity charge. The 8 steps guide describes this as lodging a quarantine entry and booking an inspection.

steps.title: Book the inspection with the local DAFF office
steps.detail: Contact the department's office at the port of arrival (Brisbane for most Queensland imports) for the inspection process and documents. Used vehicles get a full external and internal inspection. You or your broker may need to attend.
steps.timeframe: Usually within days of the car being available

steps.title: Fix any contamination
steps.detail: If risk material is found, the car must be cleaned or treated (for example fumigated) at an approved place, re-inspected, or exported or destroyed, all at your expense.
steps.cost: Cleaning and re-inspection at your cost

steps.title: Receive biosecurity release
steps.detail: Once cleared, the biosecurity direction is lifted so the ABF can release the car (if duty and taxes are also paid).

fees.label: Biosecurity charge on a full import declaration (sea)
fees.note: From 1 July 2026, collected by the ABF on goods valued over A$1,000.

fees.label: Out-of-office, weekend or public holiday
fees.note: Minimum 30 minutes, then A$93 per 15 minutes, 2026-27.

contacts.name: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (biosecurity)
contacts.note: General enquiries. To book a vehicle inspection, contact the department's local office at your arrival port (for Queensland, usually Brisbane).

watch_out: A dirty car is cleaned, fumigated, exported or destroyed at the owner's expense.
Japan's BMSB status changed recently: it was added to the emerging risk list on 1 August 2025. Check the BMSB page again for the season you ship in.
If the car is transhipped through, or the ship loads in, a BMSB target risk country (for example the USA or much of Europe), stricter measures may apply.
Ethyl formate became an approved BMSB treatment for 2026-27, onshore and offshore; offshore treatment providers must be registered under AusTreat.
Inspection time is charged in 15-minute blocks per officer, so a heavily contaminated car costs much more to clear.
Hand over the keys. Officers need to open the boot, glovebox and engine bay.

guides.title: Customs clearance, duty, GST and luxury car tax on an imported car
guides.summary: Your car is released only after an import declaration is lodged and duty, GST, any luxury car tax (LCT) and charges are paid. The general duty on passenger cars is 5%, but cars that are Japanese originating goods are duty free under the Japan-Australia Economic Partnership Agreement if you hold valid origin evidence. GST is 10% of the value of the taxable importation, and LCT is 33% of the value above the threshold (A$80,809 in 2026-27).
guides.authority: Australian Border Force; Australian Taxation Office (GST and LCT)
guides.timeframe: Lodge the declaration once the car is in transit; release usually follows quickly once approvals, biosecurity and payment are in place.
guides.cost_summary: Duty 0% (Japanese origin with evidence) or 5%; GST 10% of VoTI; LCT 33% above A$80,809 (A$91,661 fuel-efficient); import processing charge A$152 electronic for values A$10,000 and over; A$71 biosecurity charge; broker fees.
before_you_start: Have your import approval number from ROVER. The ABF will not release the car without it.
Gather the purchase invoice, auction and payment records, Japanese export or deregistration certificate, bill of lading, freight and insurance invoices, and your ID. Keep all documents for 5 years.

Get origin evidence for the JAEPA free rate: a certificate of origin from an authorised body, or an origin certification document completed by the importer, exporter or producer. It must exist when the car is imported and is valid for 12 months from issue. A car built outside Japan (even if sold in Japan) is not Japanese originating.

Expect a valuation question for a used car. The ABF says many used vehicles cannot use the price paid, and the usual method is an expert appraisal of the car's value on landing, which you arrange and pay for.
Decide whether to use a licensed customs broker (the ABF recommends one for first-time or occasional importers) or lodge yourself through the ICS or on paper at an ABF counter.

Check the air-conditioning gas. Cars with HFC-134a (or retrofitted systems holding refrigerant) may need an equipment licence unless the personal use exemption (owned over 12 months, private use) or the low volume exemption (up to 25 kg a year) applies. HFO-1234yf is not regulated. Pre-1996 CFC-12 systems are banned except under the personal use exemption.

steps.title: Engage a licensed customs broker (or get ICS access)
steps.detail: Find a licensed customs broker on the ABF list. Give them your ROVER approval, invoice, bill of lading, export certificate, origin evidence, freight and insurance details and asbestos evidence.

steps.title: Classify and value the car
steps.detail: Passenger cars are in tariff heading 8703, with separate statistical codes for used cars by engine type and size. Customs value is normally the transaction value converted to AUD at the exchange rate on the export date; for used cars that were driven before export or depreciated, an appraisal of landed value (fall-back method) is often required.

steps.title: Lodge the import declaration (N10)
steps.detail: Required for goods worth over A$1,000. Lodge electronically in the Integrated Cargo System, through a broker, or on paper (form B650 for sea cargo) at an ABF counter. Claim JAEPA preference with scheme code JEPA if the car is Japanese originating and you hold valid origin evidence.
steps.timeframe: Once the car is in transit

steps.title: Duty is worked out on the customs value
steps.detail: General rate for most used passenger cars in heading 8703: 5% of customs value. Japanese originating goods: Free under Schedule 11 of the Customs Tariff (JAEPA). Without valid origin evidence the 5% general rate applies; you may later claim a refund if you obtain a valid document.

steps.title: GST is worked out on the value of the taxable importation
steps.detail: VoTI = customs value + duty + international transport and insurance to Australia. GST = 10% of VoTI. GST-registered businesses approved for the ATO deferred GST scheme can defer it to their BAS; duty is still paid before release.

steps.title: LCT is worked out last (if the car is a luxury car)
steps.detail: LCT value = customs value + transport and insurance (if not in customs value) + duty + GST. If it exceeds the threshold, LCT = (LCT value minus threshold) x 10/11 x 33%. 2026-27 thresholds: A$80,809, or A$91,661 for fuel-efficient cars (combined 3.5 L/100 km or less from 1 July 2025). Private importers pay LCT on entry. The ATO's worked example: LCT value A$101,500 gives ($101,500 - $80,809) x 10/11 x 33% = A$6,207.30.

steps.title: Pay the Outstanding Payment Advice
steps.detail: The ABF issues an Outstanding Payment Advice with the processed declaration showing duty, GST, LCT, the import processing charge and the biosecurity charge. All duties and taxes must be paid before release.
steps.timeframe: Same day to a few days

steps.title: Get release once all agencies clear the car
steps.detail: Release needs the valid import approval, biosecurity clearance, asbestos assurance if requested, and payment. Then arrange transport (the car is unregistered; see QLD_VEHICLE_REGISTRATION for moving it).

Under-declaring the price, or claiming JAEPA for a car that is not Japanese originating, can bring short-paid duty, offences and administrative penalties.
Many used imports are valued on an appraisal of landed value, not the auction price. Budget for an appraisal if the ABF asks.

guides.title: Workshop compliance and entry on the Register of Approved Vehicles
guides.summary: A car imported under the SEVs pathway must go to a Registered Automotive Workshop (RAW), be modified to the approved Model Report so it meets the Australian Design Rules, and be checked by an Authorised Vehicle Verifier (AVV) who enters it on the Register of Approved Vehicles (RAV). Only then can it be registered. The RAV entry replaces the old compliance plate.
guides.authority: Department of Infrastructure (RVS); work done by approved RAWs and AVVs
guides.publisher: Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts
guides.timeframe: Workshop time depends on the car and the Model Report; the RAV record appears on the public search within hours of a successful submission.
guides.cost_summary: A$109 RAV entry charge for a passenger car (paid via the AVV), plus the workshop's and AVV's own charges, which are not set by government.
before_you_start: This applies to cars approved as 'Vehicle to be modified by a RAW' (usually SEVs Register cars under 25 years old). Older vehicles (25+ years) and personal effects cars are entered on the RAV through their concessional approval and do not need a RAW.

Choose your RAW before you buy: its Model Report must cover your exact make, model and variant, and its approval scope must cover the type of work. Use the ROVER public search to see each RAW's range of operations.
Choose an AVV whose service type, location and vehicle category scope fit your car. The AVV can be engaged by you, the RAW or the Model Report author.
Ask the RAW for its damage and corrosion limits and send auction sheet photos. A car over the limits cannot be complied and may have to be exported or destroyed under your approval conditions.
Get a written quote and time estimate from the RAW and ask what Queensland registration support it provides.

steps.title: Deliver the car to the RAW after customs and biosecurity release
steps.detail: Arrange transport from the wharf to the RAW. The car is unregistered; in Queensland you can tow it or use an unregistered vehicle permit (see QLD_VEHICLE_REGISTRATION).

steps.title: RAW checks identity, damage and corrosion
steps.detail: The RAW confirms the car matches the Model Report and your concessional approval, and inspects it so the threshold limits of acceptable damage or corrosion are not exceeded. If they are, the RAW must stop and notify the department.

steps.title: RAW modifies the car to the Model Report work instructions
steps.detail: Typical work is set by the Model Report so the car meets the applicable Australian Design Rules. The RAW must follow the work instructions in the required order and stop if any check fails.

steps.title: RAW signs a RAW Declaration
steps.detail: When the work is finished the RAW signs a declaration and presents the car, the declaration and supporting documents to the AVV.

steps.title: AVV verifies and submits the car to the RAV
steps.detail: The AVV verifies the car against the Model Report work instructions and submits it to the RAV. The A$109 RAV charge must be paid before the record appears on the public RAV search.

steps.title: Check the RAV entry by VIN
steps.detail: Search the RAV by VIN. New entries are transferred to the public search hourly. The RAV replaces the compliance plate, but VIN marking (ADR 61/03) still applies. Take a copy of your approval to the Queensland inspection.

fees.note: Per vehicle; RVS legislation fees and charges schedule.

fees.note: Per vehicle.

A SEVs entry or Model Report does not guarantee your particular car can be complied.
You cannot register the car in Queensland until it is on the RAV.
Do not supply (sell) the car before it is on the RAV; providing a road vehicle to the market for the first time when it is not on the RAV is an offence (120 penalty units).
Anyone with a ROVER account can report incorrect RAV information using RAV Correction.

guides.title: Registering an imported car in Queensland
guides.summary: Once your imported car is on the Register of Approved Vehicles you register it in person at a Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) customer service centre. You need a Queensland safety certificate from an approved inspection station, proof of identity and garage address, and you pay registration, the traffic improvement fee, CTP insurance and vehicle registration duty.
guides.authority: Department of Transport and Main Roads (Queensland)
guides.publisher: Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads
guides.timeframe: Usually done in one visit once the safety certificate is issued; the safety certificate is valid for 2 months or 2,000 km for a private seller.
guides.cost_summary: 12-month registration for a 4-cylinder private car A$864.50 to A$880.50 including CTP (as at 1 October 2026), plus duty of A$3 per A$100 of dutiable value (A$5 above A$100,000), plus a safety certificate inspection up to A$102.70.
before_you_start: Confirm the car is on the RAV (search by VIN) and bring a copy of your import approval. Queensland regulations accept an RAV entry as evidence the car complies; without it TMR can refuse registration.
Light vehicles under 25 years old must be right-hand drive to be registered in Queensland. Ask TMR about any special case on 13 23 80 or vehiclestandards@tmr.qld.gov.au.
Get evidence of identity (for example a Queensland driver licence) and evidence of your Queensland garage address issued within the last 6 months. First-time TMR customers also complete form F3503.
If the car has gas fittings you need a gas inspection certificate under 3 months old; if it is modified beyond its Model Report you may need a modification plate from an approved person.
Check the PPSR for the VIN if you bought the car from an Australian importer, and whether it is recorded as written off.
If you will register it in a business name, bring the business documents and an Authority to Represent (F5225) if someone else lodges for you.

steps.title: Move the car legally to the inspection
steps.detail: You can tow the car on a trailer, or drive it unregistered to the inspection station and then to the customer service centre if you carry a CTP insurance certificate for it. For other trips (for example to a repairer) apply for an unregistered vehicle permit (1 to 7 days) online with a Queensland customer reference number or with form F3523, plus class 22 CTP.

steps.title: Get a Queensland safety certificate
steps.detail: Book an approved inspection station (find one at service.transport.qld.gov.au/findais). It checks tyres, brakes, steering, suspension, body rust or damage, windscreen and lights. The certificate is needed to register an unregistered vehicle. A certificate is not required only if the car has never been registered anywhere (including Japan) and shows 500 km or less, which will not apply to a used import.
steps.timeframe: Same day if the car passes

steps.title: Buy CTP insurance
steps.detail: Choose a licensed CTP insurer. You can buy a CTP certificate before driving to inspections, or pay CTP when you register. Premiums for a private car are A$411.80 to A$427.80 for 12 months depending on insurer.

steps.title: Get a registration quote
steps.detail: Use TMR's online quote to estimate registration, traffic improvement fee and CTP for your car's cylinders and use.

guides.title: Motor dealer licence if you import cars to sell in Queensland
guides.summary: If you import Japanese cars to sell as part of a business, Queensland requires you to hold a motor dealer licence (or work for a licensed dealer). before_you_start: Decide whether this is a business. The Office of Fair Trading says anyone who trades in used motor vehicles as part of a business operation must be licensed; it sets no safe number of cars.

You must be 18 or over, complete the current required training modules from a recognised provider (older AUR99, AUR05 and AUR12 modules are not accepted), and pass suitability checks including a criminal history check.
Every business address must be registered and have a licensed person in charge.
Federal rule: providing a road vehicle to the Australian market for the first time when it is not on the RAV is an offence. Make sure each car is on the RAV before you sell it.

guides.title: Export prescribed agricultural goods: registered establishment, permits and certificates
guides.summary: Prescribed goods such as meat, dairy, fish, eggs, grain, plants and horticulture products can only be exported from Australia if they are prepared and stored at an establishment registered with the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, the exporter is registered, and an export permit (and any certificate the importing country requires) is issued through EXDOC or NEXDOC. Importing country requirements are listed in MICoR.
guides.authority: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry (DAFF), under the Export Control Act 2020
guides.publisher: Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry
guides.timeframe: Establishment registration includes a departmental audit; allow time before your first shipment. A plant export permit is typically valid for 28 days from the date the goods passed inspection.
guides.cost_summary: For 2026-27: registration applications cost A$689 (dairy, fish, egg), A$786 (grain, horticulture) or A$854 (meat), then annual registration charges from A$1,180 (horticulture grower or exporter) to over A$15,000 (large dairy), plus per-document fees (for example A$99 for an electronic horticulture phytosanitary certificate) and inspection or audit fees charged per quarter hour.
before_you_start: Classify your goods as prescribed or non-prescribed. Prescribed plant goods in shipments of up to 10 litres (liquids) or 10 kilograms (other) need no export permit, but still need inspection if the importing country requires a phytosanitary certificate.

Check the importing country's requirements in MICoR (Manual of Importing Country Requirements), then confirm them in writing with the importing country's authority (for plants, its National Plant Protection Organisation). Email any differences to the MICoR team before you export.
Contact the department's free export facilitator before applying for registration (recommended for dairy and other commodities).
Find or set up a registered establishment to prepare and store your goods.
Prepare an approved arrangement describing how the establishment meets export rules. The department checks listed staff, any outstanding Commonwealth debt, and audits the establishment.

Set up access to TradeClear, the department's online export, import and biosecurity services portal (the old exports.agriculture.gov.au Export Service address now redirects there). Export permits are created in EXDOC or NEXDOC.
Register your ABN in the ABF Integrated Cargo System and apply for access to the Single Electronic Window if you will get your EDN through NEXDOC.

steps.title: Check MICoR and confirm importing country rules
steps.detail: Look up your commodity and destination in MICoR. Confirm the requirements with the importing country's authority, because MICoR is a guide only.
steps.timeframe: Before you commit to a sale

steps.title: Register the establishment
steps.detail: Apply for establishment registration (freight forwarders, manufacturers, processors, producers and storage facilities handling prescribed goods may need it). The department checks staff and Commonwealth debts and audits the establishment against the approved arrangement.
steps.cost: A$689 to A$854 per application, then annual charges

steps.title: Register as an exporter in EXDOC
steps.detail: Register your exporter details in EXDOC, the department's export documentation system. EDI registration is open to exporters of meat, fish, dairy, eggs, grain, horticulture, skins and hides, wool and meat by-products. You need separate exporter registration if you export your own product.

steps.title: Request an export permit
steps.detail: Lodge a Request for Permit (RFP) in EXDOC (for example plants, grain, meat, fish) or a Request for Export (RFE) in NEXDOC (for example dairy). Gather evidence of eligibility such as a declaration of compliance for each shipment and transfer declarations between registered establishments.

steps.title: Book inspection by an authorised officer (plants and grain)
steps.detail: Your goods must be inspected by a plant export authorised officer (AO) appointed by the department. Book a departmental AO through a 'Request for Plant Exports Inspection Appointment', or use a third-party AO.
steps.cost: Departmental AO inspection A$98 per quarter hour; third-party AO rates are commercial

steps.title: Get the export permit and certificate
steps.detail: After inspection, request RFP authorisation and lodge any post-inspection documents. The department issues the export permit and any phytosanitary or health certificate the importing country requires through EXDOC or NEXDOC.
steps.timeframe: Plant export permits are typically valid 28 days from passing inspection

steps.title: Declare the goods to customs
steps.detail: Get your Export Declaration Number (EDN). For dairy, the department says you can obtain the EDN through NEXDOC once your ABN is registered in ICS.

guides.title: Defence export permit for military and dual-use goods, software and technology
guides.summary: If you export, supply or publish goods, software or technology listed on the Defence and Strategic Goods List (DSGL), including commercial 'dual-use' items that could have military or weapons of mass destruction uses, you need a permit from Defence Export Controls before the activity. Firearms, parts and ammunition always need a permit to export. Applications are made through the My Australian Defence Exports (MADE) portal.
guides.authority: Defence Export Controls (DEC), Department of Defence
guides.timeframe: No official processing times are published. Applications go through a completeness check, technical assessment, risk assessment and delegate review; incomplete applications get a request for information, which adds delay.
guides.cost_summary: No permit fee is mentioned on the Defence pages read.
before_you_start: Check whether your item is on the DSGL. Part 1 (Munitions List, ML1 to ML22 plus ML901 to ML910) covers items specially designed or modified for military use. Part 2 (Dual-use List, categories 0 to 9, each split into goods, test equipment, materials, software and technology) covers commercial items that could have military or WMD uses.
Use the self-help DSGL tool in the MADE portal to check control status and get recommended forms.
Even items not on the DSGL can be caught by 'catch-all' controls if there is a suspected military end-use or WMD link. Contact Defence for advice if in doubt.

Intangible supply counts: Defence has separate permit guidance for supplying DSGL technology and software intangibly, supplying it to a foreign person within Australia, certain supplies from outside Australia, and providing DSGL services outside Australia.
You need a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number (DCRN) before you apply. Registration needs a valid ABN or an ABF Cargo Client ID (CCID), and each contact needs their own email address.
Australian residents log in to MADE through ServiceConnect with a Digital ID such as myID; others use direct login.

Gather end-user and consignee details, a precise technical description of the goods or technology, and shipment quantities. Vague descriptions and missing end-user details are the most common reasons for delays.

For trade with the United States and United Kingdom, check whether you can use the AUKUS licence-free environment instead of a permit (you must be approved and lodge a notification of intent to export).

steps.title: Classify your goods, software or technology
steps.detail: Check the DSGL (2024 edition is current) using the MADE self-help tool. Note the control code. Proposed DSGL changes were under review in 2026.

steps.title: Register for a DCRN in the MADE portal
steps.detail: Log in to the My Australian Defence Exports (MADE) portal and apply for a Defence Export Controls Client Registration Number using your ABN or CCID.

steps.title: Choose the right permit type
steps.detail: Options include permits to export or supply military or dual-use goods or technology (including transhipment and repair or return), permits to supply to a foreign person in Australia, multi-party (project) permits, permits to match contracts, permits for items with in-principle approval, and renewals. Brokering needs broker registration and permits. Choosing the wrong application type is a common error.

steps.title: Lodge the application in MADE
steps.detail: All applications must be completed through MADE. Attach supporting documents (not password protected, no special characters in fields). For permits matched to a contract, give the contract name, expiry date and documentary evidence.

steps.title: Assessment and decision
steps.detail: Applications are vetted for completeness, then Stage 1 classifies the item against the DSGL and Stage 2 assesses the end user and risks against 12 legislative criteria (sanctions, human rights, security, diversion risk and international obligations). A delegate makes the decision. The application may be referred to other agencies.
steps.timeframe: Not published; can exceed a month where US ITAR items are involved (industry testimonial on a Defence page)

steps.title: Export, then keep records and report
steps.detail: Lodge an export declaration with the ABF (goods needing an export permit need one whatever their value). Keep records for 5 years from the date of supply, report transfers where a permit condition requires it, and tell DEC about changes that affect your permits.

contacts.name: DEC outreach and bulletin subscription
contacts.note: DEC runs monthly webinars and a free eLearning course, 'Navigating Australia's Defence Export Controls Framework'.

watch_out: Supplying DSGL technology or software intangibly, or to a foreign person within Australia, can need a permit even though nothing physical is shipped.
A permit is only issued if the activity would not prejudice Australia's security, defence or international relations.
Failing to keep or produce records when asked may be an offence under the Defence Trade Controls Act.
Common reasons for delays: wrong application type, special characters in fields, password-protected attachments, vague goods descriptions, and missing consignee or end-user details.
If you find you have breached the rules, Defence encourages voluntary disclosure.
Firearms, parts, accessories and ammunition always need a permit to export; Defence will only process firearms exports to Vanuatu with Port Vila Hardware as consignee.

guides.title: Lodge an export declaration and get an Export Declaration Number (EDN)
guides.summary: Before goods leave Australia you must report them to the Australian Border Force on an export declaration if they are worth more than A$2,000, need an export permit (whatever their value), are claiming duty drawback, or are dutiable goods with duty unpaid. An accepted declaration gives you an Export Declaration Number (EDN), your authority from the ABF to deal with the goods for export.
guides.authority: Australian Border Force (ABF), Department of Home Affairs
guides.timeframe: You can lodge up to six months before the export date. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within the next seven days.
guides.cost_summary: The ABF pages do not list a fee for lodging an export declaration, and there are no customs duties on exports. If you use a customs broker or freight forwarder they charge their own fee (not set by government).
before_you_start: Check whether you need one: goods worth more than A$2,000, goods needing an export permit (any value), goods where you claim duty drawback, and dutiable or excisable goods with duty or excise unpaid.

Check whether an exemption applies: personal effects, pets, goods (including mail) under A$2,000, some temporary imports under section 162A of the Customs Act 1901, diplomatic bags, Australian aircraft and ship spares, Australian Government military goods for the ADF, Australian domestic cargo, and containers for international carriage.

Check whether your goods need an export permit, for example agricultural goods (Department of Agriculture), defence and dual-use goods (Defence Export Controls), wildlife (EPBC permits), or other prohibited exports.
Decide who will lodge. The consignor (exporter, owner of the goods, or an agent for them) lodges. The ABF recommends using a licensed customs broker or agent.

If you lodge yourself, you need access to the Integrated Cargo System (ICS) and your ABN registered with the ABF, or you can lodge a paper form at an ABF counter with proof of identity and a client registration form if required.

Have the details ready: consignee, final destination country, intended export date, mode of transport, port of loading, Australian Harmonized Export Commodity Classification (AHECC) code, goods description and FOB value for each line.
Exports are generally GST-free if conditions are met; check the ATO rules.
Keep all documents for five years after lodging.

steps.title: Confirm a declaration is required
steps.detail: Use the ABF 'Export requirements' page to confirm whether the value, permit, drawback or duty rules require a declaration, or whether an exemption applies.

steps.title: Get any export permit first
steps.detail: If your goods need an export permit, get it before you lodge, because permitted goods need an EDN whatever their value and the permit details go on the declaration.

steps.title: Lodge the export declaration
steps.detail: Lodge electronically through the Integrated Cargo System (ICS), usually through a customs broker. Or lodge an Export Declaration (B957) form, with the B957a supplementary page if needed, at an ABF counter in your state or territory, with original or certified evidence of identity. One declaration covers one consignment (one consignor to one consignee).
steps.timeframe: Up to six months before export

steps.title: Receive your EDN
steps.detail: The ABF outcome is an authority to deal with the goods (your EDN), an authority with conditions, or a refusal. Keep the EDN with your shipping records; you must keep documents for five years.

steps.title: Amend or withdraw if plans change
steps.detail: Lodge amendments as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the declaration. If goods are not exported within 30 days of the intended date, withdraw the declaration within seven days after that 30-day period (electronically or with form B611). Lodge a new declaration if you export later.
steps.timeframe: Withdraw within 7 days after the 30-day window

contacts.note: The Cargo Support enquiry form is the preferred contact method.

contacts.note: Use the ABF Contact us form linked from the page.

watch_out: Not withdrawing a declaration within the required seven days is an offence.
Goods that need an export permit need an EDN even if they are worth less than A$2,000.
Lodge a separate declaration for each consignment (each consignor-to-consignee shipment).
If any details change, lodge an amendment as soon as possible, the same way you lodged the original.
Keep commercial documents for five years after lodging; the ABF can ask for them.
Some exporters can become 'Confirming Exporters' to declare estimates and confirm later (form B111), but only for certain goods.

guides.title: Export Market Development Grants (EMDG) from Austrade
guides.summary: The Export Market Development Grants program reimburses part of what small and medium Australian businesses spend on export marketing, as matched funding of A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year depending on tier. Round 4 (covering 2025-26 and 2026-27) is closed, so the practical step now is to get eligible and prepare for the next round.
guides.authority: Australian Trade and Investment Commission (Austrade)
guides.timeframe: Applications are only accepted when a round is open. Round 4 opened 12 November 2024 and tiers closed when funding ran out (Tier 2 closed the same day). No date for a next round was published on the pages read.
guides.cost_summary: No application fee is mentioned. You must be able to spend at least A$20,000 of your own money a year on eligible activities and match the grant amount with your own funds.
before_you_start: Tier 1 (ready to export, A$20,000 up to A$30,000 a year): turnover more than A$100,000 and less than A$20 million, you have not exported before, and you have completed Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test. Maximum 2 years of Tier 1.
Tier 2 (expanding in existing markets, A$20,000 up to A$50,000 a year): turnover more than A$500,000 and less than A$20 million, with evidence of recent export sales. Maximum 4 years of Tier 2.

Tier 3 (moving into new key markets, A$20,000 up to A$80,000 a year): turnover more than A$1 million and less than A$20 million, evidence of recent export sales, and a plan to enter one of 27 listed key economies (for example Japan, Singapore, the United States) where you do not already export. Maximum 4 years of Tier 3.

All tiers: a valid ABN you have traded under for at least 2 years, tax compliance, products of substantially Australian origin, and capacity to spend at least A$20,000 a year of your own (non-government) money, excluding the grant.
You can receive EMDG for up to 8 financial years in total (not necessarily consecutive). From Round 4, any year covered by a grant agreement counts, even if you report nil activity.

Eligible activities include keeping an overseas representative, short export promotion trips, consultants for research or promotion, foreign buyer visits, free samples to potential foreign buyers, and intellectual property rights. Tier 1 can include export training.
Get a Government Digital Identity and set up EMDG portal access early; Austrade says to give yourself plenty of time.

steps.title: Check your tier and read the guidelines
steps.detail: Compare your turnover and export history with the Tier 1, 2 and 3 criteria and read the EMDG grant guidelines.

steps.title: Tier 1 only: complete export training or the Export Readiness Test
steps.detail: Before applying for Tier 1 you must complete Austrade-recognised export training and/or the Export Readiness Test and keep the evidence.

steps.title: Prepare your plan to market and evidence
steps.detail: Download the sample application form and write a plan to market using the mandatory template; it must be specific to your business. Gather your ABN and proof of 2 years trading, ANZSIC code, proof of tax compliance (such as a business activity statement), evidence of Australian origin, and evidence of turnover and capacity to spend and match funds.

steps.title: Apply in the EMDG online portal when a round opens
steps.detail: Log in with your Digital Identity and lodge. Applications are assessed in the order received and tiers close when funding is fully allocated, so be ready on opening day. Not all applicants are funded.

steps.title: If funded: submit milestone reports
steps.detail: Your grant agreement sets milestone report due dates and payment schedules. For Round 4, the portal opened on 3 August 2026 for milestone reports covering 2026-27 spending. Required evidence is in Section E of your grant agreement.
steps.timeframe: As set in your grant agreement

contacts.name: Austrade EMDG
contacts.note: Subscribe to the EMDG Update newsletter to hear when the next round opens.

watch_out: Round 4 is closed. Tier 2 closed on its opening day (12 November 2024), so if a new round opens, apply as soon as it does.
EMDG is matched funding: you must fund at least A$20,000 a year yourself and match the grant amount, so plan your cash flow.
Your plan to market must be specific to your business; copied or generic plans are not accepted.
Years under a grant agreement count towards your 8-year lifetime limit even if you claim nothing.
Tier 3 markets must be new to you; markets where you already have sales do not count.
Not all eligible applicants receive funding; applications are assessed in the order received until each tier's funding runs out.
